title: Indian Economy
summary: Planning legacy, national income, RBI and monetary policy, inflation indices, the Budget, taxes and GST, flagship schemes and economic institutions. CGL asks 2-3 questions, increasingly tilted to current numbers (rates, budget, index revisions).

subtopics.title: National income, growth and base years
subtopics.concept:
### National income concepts
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| GDP | Market value of all final goods & services produced **within India** in a year |
| GNP | GDP + net factor income from abroad (NFIA) |
| NNP | GNP − depreciation |
| Per capita income | NNP ÷ population |
| Factor cost vs market price | Market price = factor cost + indirect taxes − subsidies |
| Nominal vs real GDP | Real GDP is at constant prices; **GDP deflator = (Nominal ÷ Real) × 100** |

### Bodies
- **NSO** (National Statistical Office, under **MoSPI**, formed 2019 by merging CSO + NSSO) estimates GDP and CPI-IIP series.
- **Economic Survey** — by the Department of Economic Affairs (Finance Ministry), released a day before the Budget.

### Base-year wave of 2026 (very exam-relevant)
| Indicator | Old base | New base | Release |
|---|---|---|---|
| GDP / National Accounts | 2011-12 | **2022-23** | 27 Feb 2026 (MoSPI) |
| CPI | 2012 | **2024** | 12 Feb 2026 (MoSPI) |
| IIP | 2011-12 | **2022-23** | effective 1 Jun 2026 (28-day lag) |
| WPI | 2011-12 | **2022-23** | 15 Jun 2026 (DPIIT); items raised **697 → 957**; Producer Price Indices (PPI) introduced — WPI to run alongside PPI for 5 years |

Economy sectors: primary (agriculture, mining), secondary (manufacturing), tertiary (services). India is a **services-led** economy (over half of GVA).

subtopics.notes:
### Counting the economy — the national income family
**GDP (Gross Domestic Product)** is the market value of all **final** goods and services produced **within India** in a year — by Indians or foreigners. **GNP** adds what Indians earn abroad: **GNP = GDP + Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA)** — remittances, profits, interest flowing in minus the same flowing out. **NNP = GNP − depreciation** (wear and tear of machines). **National Income** in exam language = **NNP at factor cost**. **Per capita income** = national income ÷ population. Moving between prices: **Market Price = Factor Cost + indirect taxes − subsidies**, because indirect taxes push the price up and subsidies hold it down.

Chains to memorise:
- GDP → (+NFIA) → GNP → (−depreciation) → NNP → (−indirect taxes, +subsidies) → National Income (NNP at FC).
- NNP at factor cost is the textbook definition of 'national income'; GNP is the widest of the family.

### Nominal, real and the deflator
**Nominal (current-price) GDP** uses this year's prices, so it grows even if only prices grow. **Real (constant-price) GDP** uses a fixed **base year's** prices, so it shows real production. The bridge is the **GDP deflator**:

$$\text{Deflator} = \frac{\text{Nominal GDP}}{\text{Real GDP}} \times 100$$

If nominal GDP is ₹330 and real GDP is ₹300, the deflator is 110 — prices rose 10% since the base year. Divide nominal by (deflator ÷ 100) to recover real GDP. Base years are **revised periodically**: the older national accounts series used **2011-12**, and MoSPI released a **new series with base year 2022-23** in February 2026 (the IIP followed with the same base from June 2026). Exams frame base-year questions around exactly this revision.

### How it is measured
Three equivalent approaches: the **income method** (wages + rent + interest + profit), the **expenditure method** (private consumption + investment + government spending + net exports: $C + I + G + (X-M)$) and the **product (value-added) method** (output sector by sector, counting only **value added** to avoid double counting). India now anchors sectoral reporting on **Gross Value Added (GVA) at basic prices**, with GDP = GVA + product taxes − product subsidies. The statistical agency is the **National Statistical Office (NSO)** under **MoSPI** (the old CSO and NSSO were merged into it in 2019). Estimates come in stages — advance, provisional, revised, final.

### The three sectors
**Primary** = agriculture, forestry, fishing, mining; **secondary** = manufacturing, construction, electricity; **tertiary (services)** = trade, transport, finance, IT, public administration. Services contribute the biggest share of India's GVA today, which is why exams test sector shares and which activity belongs to which sector. Related small facts: the **eight core industries** (coal, crude oil, natural gas, refinery products, fertilisers, steel, cement, electricity) feed the Index of Eight Core Industries and carry a large weight in the IIP; **per capita income** here means per capita **net national income**, not GDP per head.

### Quick revision
- GDP = within India; GNP = GDP + NFIA; NNP = GNP − depreciation; National Income = NNP at factor cost.
- MP = FC + indirect taxes − subsidies; deflator = (nominal ÷ real) × 100.
- Real GDP uses base-year prices; the current family of series moved to **base year 2022-23** (released Feb 2026), replacing 2011-12.
- Methods: income, expenditure ($C+I+G+X-M$), value-added; GVA at basic prices; NSO under MoSPI (CSO + NSSO merged 2019).
- Sectors: primary / secondary / tertiary; services now the largest GVA share.
- Eight core industries: coal, crude, gas, refinery, fertilisers, steel, cement, electricity.

patterns.name: GDP–GNP–NNP chains and definitions
patterns.howToSpot: 'GNP equals', 'national income means NNP at factor cost', 'which is the largest measure', statement sets mixing the four aggregates.
patterns.logic:
1. Build the ladder in one line: GDP → +NFIA → GNP → −depreciation → NNP → −indirect taxes + subsidies → National Income.
2. The widest measure is GNP (when NFIA is positive); 'national income' in exams = **NNP at factor cost**.
3. Watch the trap: GDP excludes NFIA entirely — an option calling GDP 'income of residents at home and abroad' is wrong.

example.q: If GDP is ₹100 and net factor income from abroad is ₹5, GNP equals —
example.solution: **₹105** — GNP = GDP + NFIA; here income earned abroad by residents exceeds what foreigners earn here by 5.

patterns.name: Nominal vs real GDP and the deflator
patterns.howToSpot: Numbers for nominal and real GDP are given and the deflator (or real growth) is asked, or statements compare the two concepts.
patterns.logic:
1. Deflator = (Nominal ÷ Real) × 100. Compute in one step; the answer is an index number with base year = 100.
2. Real GDP = Nominal ÷ (deflator ÷ 100).
3. Real GDP can fall while nominal rises — that is exactly what a high deflator means.

example.q: Nominal GDP is ₹330 lakh crore and real GDP ₹300 lakh crore. The GDP deflator is —
example.solution: (330 ÷ 300) × 100 = **110** — the price level stands 10% above the base year.

patterns.name: Base years and the new series
patterns.howToSpot: 'The new GDP series has which base year', 'which agency releases national accounts', 'the old base was', questions on the 2022-23 / 2011-12 shift.
patterns.logic:
1. Old bases: GDP and IIP **2011-12**, CPI **2012**; the new national accounts series uses **2022-23** (released February 2026), with IIP re-based alongside.
2. Release authority: **NSO under MoSPI** — the CSO and NSSO were merged into the NSO in 2019.
3. A base year is a reference year whose prices equal 100; both real GDP and indices are measured against it.

example.q: India's national accounts statistics are released by —
example.solution: The **National Statistical Office (NSO)** under the **Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI)** — the merged successor of the CSO and NSSO.

patterns.name: Per capita income and measurement methods
patterns.howToSpot: 'Per capita income is calculated from', 'the expenditure method adds', which method uses wages-rent-interest-profit.
patterns.logic:
1. Per capita income = national income (NNP at FC) ÷ population — not GDP ÷ population.
2. Methods: income = wages + rent + interest + profit; expenditure = $C + I + G + (X-M)$; value-added = sector-wise GVA.
3. Double counting is avoided by counting only **value added** at each stage.

example.q: The **expenditure method** of measuring national income adds up —
example.solution: Private final consumption + investment + government expenditure + net exports, i.e. $C + I + G + (X - M)$. The income method instead sums factor incomes.

patterns.name: Sectors, GVA and core industries
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which activity belongs to the tertiary sector', 'GVA is measured at which prices', the eight core industries list.
patterns.logic:
1. Sectors: primary (agriculture, mining), secondary (manufacturing, construction), tertiary (services).
2. GVA is measured at **basic prices**; GDP = GVA + product taxes − product subsidies.
3. Eight core industries: coal, crude oil, natural gas, refinery products, fertilisers, steel, cement, electricity — electricity and refinery carry large weights.

example.q: Under the GVA framework, **GDP** is obtained by —
example.solution: Adding **product taxes** and subtracting **product subsidies** from GVA at basic prices.

subtopics.title: Five Year Plans and NITI Aayog
subtopics.concept:
### Five Year Plans (1951-2017)
| Plan | Period | Highlight / model |
|---|---|---|
| 1st | 1951-56 | Agriculture priority; based on Harrod-Domar model |
| 2nd | 1956-61 | **Mahalanobis model** — heavy industries |
| 3rd | 1961-66 | Self-reliance; wars and drought derailed it |
| Plan Holiday | 1966-69 | Three Annual Plans (after 1962/1965 wars) |
| 4th | 1969-74 | "Growth with stability"; 14 banks nationalised (1969) |
| 5th | 1974-79 | **Garibi Hatao**; terminated early |
| Rolling Plan | 1978-80 | Janata government concept (D.T. Lakdawala) |
| 6th | 1980-85 | Poverty removal focus; IRDP/NREP start |
| 7th | 1985-90 | Food, work, productivity |
| Annual Plans | 1990-92 | Transition years |
| 8th | 1992-97 | Ran against **LPG reforms** (1991 crisis) |
| 9th | 1997-2002 | "Growth with social justice" |
| 10th | 2002-07 | 8% target |
| 11th | 2007-12 | "Faster and more inclusive growth" |
| 12th (last) | 2012-17 | "Faster, more inclusive, sustainable growth" |

### NITI Aayog (since 1 January 2015)
Replaced the Planning Commission (set up 1950, Nehru). Created by a **Cabinet resolution** — neither constitutional nor statutory. PM chairs it; Governing Council of CMs/LG administrators; Vice-Chair **A.K. Lahiri** (since May 2026); CEO **Anurag Jain** (since Aug 2026). Works through a 15-year Vision, 7-year Strategy and 3-year Action Agenda; runs indices like the SDG India Index, Composite Water Management Index and Aspirational Districts Programme.

tricks.title: Plan-era story line
tricks.body: 1-farm (1951) → 2-machines (Mahalanobis) → 3-wars → holiday (66-69) → 4-stability + bank nationalisation → 5-Garibi Hatao → rolling (Janata) → 6-7 growth → 8-reforms (1992) → 9-12 inclusive → NITI (2015).

example.q: Which plan coincided with the LPG reforms?
example.solution: The 8th Plan (1992-97).

tricks.title: Plan-break tags
tricks.body: Two gaps: **Plan Holiday 1966-69** (wars/drought) and **Annual Plans 1990-92** (transition after the 8th was delayed).

example.q: Why was there a 'Plan Holiday'?
example.solution: 1962 and 1965 wars plus drought deranged the 3rd Plan; 1966-69 ran as annual plans.

mistakes: Saying NITI Aayog is statutory — it is a Cabinet-resolution body.
Crediting the 2nd Plan to Harrod-Domar — the 1st Plan's framework was Harrod-Domar; Mahalanobis belongs to the 2nd.
Assuming the 12th Plan ended early — it ran full term to 2017; NITI then took over.
subtopics.notes:
### From plans to NITI
India adopted planning after independence; the **Planning Commission** was set up on **15 March 1950** by a **Cabinet resolution** (not a statute) with the **Prime Minister as chairman**. It steered **twelve Five Year Plans** from 1951 to 2017. From **1 January 2015** a **Cabinet resolution** replaced it with **NITI Aayog** (National Institution for Transforming India) — a think tank, not a fund-allocating plan body.

### The plan ladder — who believed in what
| Plan | Period | Signature idea |
|---|---|---|
| 1st | 1951-56 | **Harrod-Domar model**; agriculture and irrigation priority |
| 2nd | 1956-61 | **P.C. Mahalanobis model**; heavy industry and capital goods |
| 3rd | 1961-66 | 'Gadgil strategy'; self-reliance; broken by wars and drought |
| Plan Holiday | 1966-69 | Three **annual plans** after the 3rd failed |
| 4th | 1969-74 | 'Growth with stability'; family planning pushed |
| 5th | 1974-78 | Poverty removal ('Garibi Hatao'); terminated early |
| Rolling plan | 1978-80 | The **rolling plan** concept (D.T. Lakdawala) |
| 6th | 1980-85 | Poverty eradication first; IRDP, NREP begin |
| 7th | 1985-90 | Food, work, productivity; Jawahar Rozgar Yojana (1989) |
| Annual plans | 1990-92 | Transition years, economic crisis |
| 8th | 1992-97 | Launched alongside the **1991 reforms** (LPG) |
| 9th | 1997-2002 | 'Growth with social justice and equality' |
| 10th | 2002-07 | 8% growth target; monitoring |
| 11th | 2007-12 | '**Faster and more inclusive growth**' |
| 12th | 2012-17 | 'Faster, more inclusive and **sustainable** growth' — the last plan |

Memory hooks: 2nd plan = Mahalanobis = machines; 8th plan began with liberalisation; 11th = inclusive; 12th = sustainable; the words 'plan holiday' and 'rolling plan' belong to 1966-69 and 1978-80 respectively.

### NITI Aayog — structure and work
The **Prime Minister chairs** NITI Aayog. Its **Governing Council** brings together all Chief Ministers and Lt Governors of UTs; a **Vice-Chairperson** and full-time members are appointed by the PM; a **CEO** runs day-to-day work. Its design philosophy is **cooperative federalism** (states as partners) and **competitive federalism** (states ranked and nudged). Instead of plans it produces planning documents: a **15-year vision**, a **7-year strategy** and a **3-year action agenda**. Its visible products are the indices and programmes exams quote: the **SDG India Index**, the **Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI)** for states, the **Aspirational Districts Programme (2018, 112 districts)**, the Composite Water Management Index, and school/health innovation reports. Contrast lines asked in exams: Planning Commission allocated plan funds and made five-year plans; NITI Aayog is advisory, does not allocate funds, and works through indices, evidence and monitoring.

### Why this subtopic scores
Questions stay at the level of models, years, themes and NITI structure — all stable facts. Learn one phrase per plan, the two annual-plan interludes, and the three NITI documents, and you can crack any match-the-column on this page.

### Quick revision
- Planning Commission: 15 March 1950, Cabinet resolution, PM as chairman; 12 plans, 1951-2017.
- 1st = Harrod-Domar/agriculture; 2nd = Mahalanobis/heavy industry; Plan Holiday 1966-69; Rolling plan 1978-80.
- 8th = LPG reforms era; 11th = inclusive growth; 12th (2012-17) = last plan, 'sustainable'.
- NITI Aayog: 1 Jan 2015, Cabinet resolution; PM chairs; Governing Council = CMs + LGs; CEO + Vice-Chairperson.
- Documents: 15-year vision, 7-year strategy, 3-year action agenda; no fund allocation.
- Flagship indices: SDG India Index, state MPI, Aspirational Districts (2018).

patterns.name: Plan ↔ model matching
patterns.howToSpot: 'The Second Five Year Plan was based on', 'the Harrod-Domar model belongs to which plan', matching thinkers and plans.
patterns.logic:
1. Two pairs carry all the marks: **1st plan — Harrod-Domar** (agriculture focus) and **2nd plan — P.C. Mahalanobis** (heavy industry).
2. The 3rd plan's strategy is attributed to **D.R. Gadgil**.
3. If the question names 'heavy industry' or 'capital goods', the answer is the Mahalanobis model of the 2nd plan (1956-61).

example.q: The **Mahalanobis model**, emphasising heavy industry, was the basis of which plan?
example.solution: The **Second Five Year Plan (1956-61)** — it pushed capital-goods and machine-building industries behind public-sector investment.

patterns.name: Plan ↔ years ↔ theme
patterns.howToSpot: 'Growth with stability was the theme of', 'which plan coincided with the 1991 reforms', ordering of plans or spotting the last plan.
patterns.logic:
1. Theme hooks: 4th = growth with stability; 9th = growth with social justice; 11th = inclusive growth; 12th = faster, inclusive and sustainable — the **last plan (2012-17)**.
2. The **8th plan (1992-97)** opened in the liberalisation era; its start was delayed by two annual plans (1990-92).
3. Interludes: Plan Holiday 1966-69 (after the 3rd); Rolling Plan 1978-80.

example.q: 'Growth with stability' was the stated objective of which Five Year Plan?
example.solution: The **Fourth Plan (1969-74)** — it sought growth while controlling the inflation that followed the wars and droughts of the 1960s.

patterns.name: NITI Aayog structure and documents
patterns.howToSpot: 'Who chairs NITI Aayog', 'the Governing Council consists of', 'the 15-year vision / 7-year strategy / 3-year action agenda', statements on NITI's powers.
patterns.logic:
1. Chairs: the **Prime Minister**; day-to-day work by a **CEO**; think-tank headship by a **Vice-Chairperson**.
2. **Governing Council = all Chief Ministers + Lt Governors of UTs** — the federalism showcase.
3. Documents: **15-year vision, 7-year strategy, 3-year action agenda**; NITI does **not** allocate plan funds.

example.q: The **Governing Council** of NITI Aayog includes —
example.solution: The Prime Minister (chair), the **Chief Ministers of all states** and the **Lt Governors of Union Territories** — making it the main centre-state planning forum.

patterns.name: Planning Commission vs NITI Aayog
patterns.howToSpot: Statement pairs: fund allocation, statutory vs executive origin, plan body vs think tank, year of replacement.
patterns.logic:
1. Both were created by **Cabinet resolution** — neither is statutory or constitutional.
2. Planning Commission (15 March 1950) allocated funds and made plans; NITI Aayog (1 January 2015) advises, monitors and builds indices.
3. The Finance Commission — a constitutional body — is the body people confuse with both; it handles tax devolution, not planning.

example.q: Which statement about NITI Aayog is **correct**?
example.solution: It was set up on 1 January 2015 by a **Cabinet resolution**, replacing the Planning Commission as an advisory **think tank** — it neither allocates plan funds nor enjoys statutory status.

patterns.name: Plan Holiday, rolling plan and annual plans
patterns.howToSpot: 'The Plan Holiday occurred during', 'the rolling plan concept is associated with', which plans were cut short.
patterns.logic:
1. **Plan Holiday: 1966-69** — three annual plans after the 3rd plan collapsed under war and drought.
2. **Rolling plan: 1978-80** (concept credited to D.T. Lakdawala) — plans revised every year with a moving horizon.
3. Annual plans also ran in **1990-92** before the delayed 8th plan; the 5th plan (1974-78) was terminated a year early by the Janata government.

example.q: The '**Plan Holiday**' in Indian planning refers to —
example.solution: The years **1966-69**, when three **annual plans** replaced the usual five-year plan after the third plan was derailed by wars and drought.

subtopics.title: Money, banking and the RBI
subtopics.concept:
### Reserve Bank of India
Established **1 April 1935** under the **RBI Act, 1934** (Hilton Young Commission 1926); **nationalised 1 January 1949**; HQ **Mumbai**. Governor: **Sanjay Malhotra** (26th, since December 2024). Original capital shareholders included private hands until 1949; RBI is the currency issuer, banker to banks and to the government, and manages exchange reserves.

### Monetary Policy Committee (2016)
**6 members** (3 RBI incl. Governor with casting vote + 3 Government nominees); meets at least 4 times a year; mandate — CPI inflation **4% ± 2%**.

### Policy rates (after the 5 August 2026 MPC — held unchanged, neutral stance)
| Rate | Level | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **Repo** | **5.25%** | Lending rate of RBI to banks (policy rate) |
| **SDF** | 5.00% | Floor; RBI borrows from banks at repo − 0.25% |
| **MSF / Bank Rate** | 5.50% | Ceiling; repo + 0.25% |
| **CRR** | **3.00%** | Cut from 4% in four 25-bp tranches (Sep–Nov 2025); earns banks nothing |
| **SLR** | 18% | Minimum share of deposits in gold/G-secs |
| Reverse repo | 3.35% | Dormant as operative rate since SDF's introduction (2022) |

Quantitative tools also include OMOs, USD/INR swaps, and VRR/VRRR auctions. **Cut CRR/repo → cheaper money → more liquidity; raise → inflation control.**

### Banking history
| Event | Year / fact |
|---|---|
| RBI set up | 1935; nationalised 1949 |
| SBI created (Imperial Bank → SBI) | **1955** |
| **14** banks nationalised (deposits ≥ ₹50 cr) | **19 July 1969** |
| **6** more banks (≥ ₹200 cr) | 15 April 1980 |
| RRBs started (Narasimham working group) | 1975 |
| Narasimham Committee I / II | 1991 / 1998 — banking-sector reforms, prudential norms |
| Nachiket Mor Committee | 2014 — financial inclusion, payments banks |

tricks.title: Corridor arithmetic
tricks.body: Repo is the middle: SDF = repo − 0.25 (floor), MSF = Bank Rate = repo + 0.25 (ceiling). With repo 5.25 → 5.00 / 5.25 / 5.50.

example.q: If repo were 6.00%, what would the MSF be?
example.solution: 6.25% — always repo + 25 bp.

tricks.title: Nationalisation anchors
tricks.body: 1935 born, 1949 nationalised (RBI), 1955 SBI, 1969 fourteen, 1975 RRBs, 1980 six.

example.q: How many banks in the 1980 round?
example.solution: Six (deposits ≥ ₹200 crore).

tricks.title: MPC fixed points
tricks.body: 6 members; 4 meetings a year minimum; target CPI 4% ± 2%; Governor's casting vote.

example.q: Who has the casting vote in the MPC?
example.solution: The RBI Governor.

mistakes: Repeating pre-2026 rates — repo is 5.25%, CRR 3%, not 6.5%/4%.
Confusing reverse repo (3.35%, dormant) with SDF (5.00%, the operative floor).
Crediting the Nachiket Mor committee with banking reforms of the 1990s — those were Narasimham I/II.
subtopics.notes:
### The Reserve Bank of India — the monetary authority
The RBI was set up under the **RBI Act, 1934** and began work on **1 April 1935** (headquarters then Calcutta, moved to **Mumbai** in 1937). It was **nationalised on 1 January 1949** — the same year the Banking Regulation Act arrived. It is the **central bank**: sole issuer of currency (except the **₹1 note and coins**, issued by the Government of India's Finance Ministry), banker to the government, banker to banks and **lender of last resort**, custodian of forex reserves, and regulator of banks and payment systems.

### The policy toolkit
- **Repo rate**: the rate at which the RBI lends short-term to banks against securities — the main **policy rate**.
- **Standing Deposit Facility (SDF)**: since April 2020 the **floor** of the corridor — banks park surplus funds with the RBI **without collateral**, at repo **− 25 basis points**.
- **Marginal Standing Facility (MSF)**: the **ceiling** at repo **+ 25 basis points**; banks may dip into it at night borrowing above their SLR holdings. The **Bank Rate** equals the MSF.
- **CRR (Cash Reserve Ratio)**: the share of deposits banks must keep **as cash with the RBI** — earns no interest. **SLR (Statutory Liquidity Ratio)**: the share kept in **liquid assets** (governments securities, gold) with the bank itself. The RBI moves CRR/SLR to absorb or release liquidity.
- **Open Market Operations (OMOs)**, LAF auctions, and forex swaps fine-tune liquidity daily.

### The Monetary Policy Committee
Since the **RBI (Amendment) Act, 2016**, policy decisions rest with a **six-member MPC** — three from the RBI (the Governor with a **casting vote**) and three outside members appointed by the government. It meets **bi-monthly** and targets **CPI inflation of 4% with a ±2% band**; missing the band for **three consecutive quarters** triggers a report to the government. The framework's nominal anchor is **headline CPI**, not WPI.

### Money supply and bank history
Money stock tiers: **M1 = currency with the public + demand deposits with banks + other deposits with the RBI** (narrow money); M2 = M1 + post-office savings; **M3 = M1 + time deposits** (broad money — the headline aggregate); M4 = M3 + post-office deposits (excluding NSCs). History pins: **SBI** = Imperial Bank of India nationalised in **1955**; its subsidiaries came in 1959. **14 major private banks nationalised on 19 July 1969** and **six more in April 1980**. **Regional Rural Banks** began in **1975** (first: Prathama Grameen Bank). Deposit insurance runs through the **DICGC** (limit **₹5 lakh** per depositor per bank since 2020). **NPCI (2008)** built UPI, RuPay, IMPS and FASTag rails; **payment banks** and **small finance banks** followed the **Nachiket Mor committee (2014)** — payment banks take deposits but cannot lend.

### Quick revision
- RBI Act 1934; working 1 April 1935; nationalised 1 Jan 1949; HQ Mumbai; issues all currency except ₹1 note and coins.
- Corridor: SDF = repo − 25 bp (floor); MSF = Bank Rate = repo + 25 bp (ceiling).
- CRR = cash with RBI; SLR = liquid assets with the bank; OMO = buying/selling G-secs.
- MPC: 6 members (3 RBI, Governor casting vote), bi-monthly, CPI 4% ± 2%, breach = 3 quarters.
- M1 = currency + demand deposits + other RBI deposits; M3 = M1 + time deposits.
- 1955 SBI; 1969 (14 banks); 1980 (6 banks); 1975 RRBs; DICGC ₹5 lakh; NPCI 2008 (UPI 2016).

patterns.name: RBI identity, history and currency facts
patterns.howToSpot: 'The RBI was established under which Act', 'when was it nationalised', 'which note does the RBI not issue', 'where is its headquarters'.
patterns.logic:
1. Anchors: RBI Act **1934**, operations from **1 April 1935**, nationalised **1 January 1949**, HQ **Mumbai**.
2. Currency split: RBI issues ₹2 and above; the **₹1 note and all coins** come from the **Finance Ministry**.
3. The RBI is the bankers' bank and **lender of last resort** — commercial banks are its clients, not the public.

example.q: The **one-rupee note** in India is issued by —
example.solution: The **Government of India (Finance Ministry)** — the RBI issues all other denominations; coins are also minted by the government.

patterns.name: Policy rates and the corridor
patterns.howToSpot: 'SDF is how much below the repo rate', 'the bank rate equals', 'which rate is the policy rate', matching rate ↔ instrument.
patterns.logic:
1. Learn the corridor as positions, not numbers: **SDF = repo − 25 bp (floor)**; **MSF = Bank Rate = repo + 25 bp (ceiling)**.
2. Repo = RBI lends to banks (policy rate); SDF = banks park surplus without collateral; MSF = emergency overnight borrowing.
3. CRR and SLR are ratios, not rates — do not call them 'policy rates'.

example.q: The **Standing Deposit Facility (SDF)** is placed —
example.solution: **25 basis points below the repo rate** — the corridor floor where banks deposit surplus liquidity with the RBI without providing collateral.

patterns.name: Monetary Policy Committee and the inflation target
patterns.howToSpot: 'How many members sit on the MPC', 'who holds the casting vote', 'the inflation target is', 'how often does the MPC meet'.
patterns.logic:
1. **6 members**: three from the RBI (the Governor, a Deputy Governor and one RBI officer) and three outside experts appointed by the government. The **Governor has the casting vote**.
2. Target: **CPI 4% ± 2%**; meetings **bi-monthly**; failure = 3 consecutive quarters outside the band.
3. Legal base: RBI (Amendment) Act, **2016**; the WPI is not the target.

example.q: The **casting vote** in the Monetary Policy Committee belongs to —
example.solution: The **RBI Governor** — with six members, a 3-3 split is broken by the Governor's casting vote.

patterns.name: CRR, SLR and liquidity tools
patterns.howToSpot: 'CRR is kept with', 'SLR consists of', 'which tool releases liquidity immediately', statement sets contrasting CRR and SLR.
patterns.logic:
1. **CRR** = cash **with the RBI**, no interest; **SLR** = the bank's own holdings of G-secs/gold/other approved liquid assets.
2. Cutting CRR or SLR, buying G-secs (OMO), or lowering repo — each injects ease; the reverse tightens.
3. The MSF ceiling exists so banks in stress can borrow overnight even beyond SLR holdings.

example.q: The **Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)** requires banks to keep —
example.solution: A fixed share of their net demand and time liabilities **as cash balances with the RBI**, on which no interest is paid.

patterns.name: Money supply tiers and banking milestones
patterns.howToSpot: 'M1 consists of', 'which is the broad money measure', '14 banks were nationalised in', 'the first RRB was', DICGC and NPCI facts.
patterns.logic:
1. M1 = currency with public + **demand deposits** + other deposits with RBI; **M3 = M1 + time deposits** = broad money.
2. Bank history: SBI 1955 (Imperial Bank); **1969 = 14 banks**; **1980 = 6 banks**; RRBs 1975 (Prathama).
3. Systems: DICGC insurance **₹5 lakh**; NPCI (2008) runs UPI/RuPay/IMPS; payment banks (Nachiket Mor) take deposits, cannot lend.

example.q: Which of the following is included in **M1** but not in M3?
example.solution: Nothing — **M3 is M1 plus time deposits**, so every M1 component sits inside M3. Watch such trap options carefully in 'narrow vs broad money' questions.

subtopics.title: Inflation and price indices
subtopics.concept:
### Inflation types
| Type | Cause |
|---|---|
| Demand-pull | Excess demand chasing goods |
| Cost-push | Rising input costs (oil, wages) |
| Stagflation | High inflation + stagnant growth + unemployment |
| Disinflation | Falling rate of inflation (still positive) |
| Deflation | Falling price level |
| Hyperinflation | Triple-digit monthly runaways |

### Measurement (post-2026 base revisions)
| Index | Compiler | Base | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **CPI-Combined** (headline) | **NSO, MoSPI** | **2024** (new series from Feb 2026) | Rural + urban; anchors MPC's 4±2% target |
| **WPI** | Office of Economic Adviser, **DPIIT** | **2022-23** (from 15 Jun 2026) | Headline basket 957 items; excludes services; being replaced by PPIs over 5 years |
| IIP | NSO | 2022-23 (from 1 Jun 2026) | Monthly industrial output, 28-day lag |
| GDP deflator | NSO | ratio | Nominal/real GDP × 100 |

- **Core inflation** = headline CPI minus food and fuel.
- Inflation targeting framework: RBI Act amended **2016** (MPC), target **4% CPI ± 2%**, failure band defined as three consecutive quarters outside range.
- CPI food measure: **CFPI**; WPI fuel & power and manufactured products are the volatile groups; RBI uses CPI (not WPI) for policy.

tricks.title: Index-compiler pairs
tricks.body: CPI-IIP-GDP = MoSPI/NSO; WPI-PPI = DPIIT's Office of Economic Adviser. 'M for MoSPI, W for DPIIT(OEA)'.

example.q: Who compiles the WPI?
example.solution: Office of Economic Adviser, DPIIT (Commerce & Industry Ministry).

tricks.title: Core = strip the volatile
tricks.body: Core inflation = headline − food − fuel. Stagflation = stagnation + inflation together.

example.q: If headline CPI is 6%, food & fuel contribute 2.5%, what is core?
example.solution: About 3.5%.

mistakes: Using WPI for the inflation target — the MPC targets **CPI**.
Giving WPI the old 2011-12 base — since 15 June 2026 it is 2022-23 (957 items).
Calling disinflation 'deflation' — disinflation is only a slower rise, deflation is a fall.
subtopics.notes:
### What inflation is
Inflation is a **sustained rise in the general price level** — the same ₹100 buys less over time. Its two engines: **demand-pull** (too much money chasing too few goods — often after tax cuts, cheap credit or high government spending) and **cost-push** (costlier inputs — oil, fertiliser, wages — push prices up even when demand is soft). Related labels: **deflation** (falling prices), **disinflation** (inflation falling but still positive), **stagflation** (high inflation + stagnating growth), **headline inflation** (all items) vs **core inflation** (headline minus food and fuel — the 'underlying' trend).

### The price indices — who measures what
| Index | Agency | Base year status |
|---|---|---|
| **CPI (Combined)** — headline, rural, urban | **NSO, MoSPI** | old base **2012**; new series with base **2024** released February 2026 |
| **WPI** | Office of Economic Adviser, **DPIIT** (Commerce Ministry) | old base **2011-12**; new series **2022-23** launched June 2026 with a wider basket (697 → 957 items) and new **Producer Price Indices** |
| **CPI-IW** (industrial workers) | **Labour Bureau** | used for dearness allowance |
| CPI-AL / CPI-RL (agri/rural labourers) | Labour Bureau | — |
| **IIP** (industrial output, not prices) | NSO | old base 2011-12; re-based to **2022-23** from June 2026 |

Key contrasts exams test: the **WPI covers only goods — no services** — and measures prices at the **wholesale/producer** stage; the **CPI measures retail prices** paid by consumers and includes services. Since 2016 the RBI's inflation target is framed on **CPI**, not WPI. The **Eight Core Industries index** (coal, crude oil, natural gas, refinery, fertilisers, steel, cement, electricity) is a high-frequency output series feeding the IIP.

### Reading the numbers
CPI/WPI changes are reported as **year-on-year** per cent. Food and beverages carry the largest weight in the CPI basket, which is why a monsoon shock moves headline inflation sharply while core stays steadier — a favourite statement question. The **GDP deflator** (nominal ÷ real × 100) is the economy-wide price gauge used in national accounts. For fiscal policy, the government watches inflation because it drives **dearness allowance**, indexation and subsidy bills.

### Quick revision
- Demand-pull = excess demand; cost-push = input costs; stagflation = inflation + stagnation; core = headline − food & fuel.
- CPI = retail, includes services, NSO/MoSPI; new base year 2024 (Feb 2026). WPI = wholesale, goods only, DPIIT; new base 2022-23 (Jun 2026) + PPIs.
- CPI-IW/AL/RL = Labour Bureau (DA linkage uses CPI-IW).
- RBI targets CPI (4% ± 2%), never WPI.
- IIP = industrial production (re-based 2022-23); eight core industries feed it.
- Deflation = falling prices; disinflation = slower positive inflation.

patterns.name: Identify the inflation type
patterns.howToSpot: A story (oil price shock, monsoon failure, credit boom) is given and the type — demand-pull or cost-push — is asked; sometimes deflation/stagflation options appear.
patterns.logic:
1. Ask: did demand rise (tax cuts, cheap loans, spending) → **demand-pull**; or did costs rise (crude, wages, inputs) → **cost-push**.
2. Stagflation = inflation **plus** stagnant growth — cost-push shocks often produce it.
3. Deflation = general prices **falling**; disinflation = inflation slowing but positive.

example.q: A sharp rise in **imported crude oil prices** pushing up general prices is an example of —
example.solution: **Cost-push inflation** — the input-cost shock passes into transport, manufacturing and retail prices even without excess demand.

patterns.name: Index ↔ agency ↔ coverage
patterns.howToSpot: 'The WPI is compiled by', 'which index does the RBI target', 'which index covers services', agency and coverage matching.
patterns.logic:
1. Agencies: CPI (Combined) — **NSO/MoSPI**; WPI — **Office of Economic Adviser (DPIIT)**; CPI-IW/AL/RL — **Labour Bureau**.
2. Coverage: WPI = **goods only, wholesale stage, no services**; CPI = **retail, includes services**.
3. The RBI's 4 ± 2% target uses **CPI**, never WPI.

example.q: The **Wholesale Price Index** in India is released by —
example.solution: The **Office of Economic Adviser** in the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (Commerce & Industry Ministry) — not the NSO.

patterns.name: Base years and new series
patterns.howToSpot: 'The new CPI series uses which base year', 'the WPI basket was expanded to', 'the IIP base', matching index ↔ base year.
patterns.logic:
1. New anchors: CPI base **2024** (from February 2026); WPI and IIP base **2022-23** (WPI series June 2026, IIP from June 2026); old bases were 2012 (CPI) and 2011-12 (WPI/IIP).
2. The 2026 WPI revision enlarged the basket from **697 to 957 items** and launched **Producer Price Indices** alongside.
3. A base year's index = 100; a series revision resets weights to a recent consumption/production structure.

example.q: The new **Consumer Price Index** series released in February 2026 has base year —
example.solution: **2024** — replacing the 2012 base; GDP and WPI/IIP use the fiscal-year base 2022-23 instead.

patterns.name: Core vs headline and related terms
patterns.howToSpot: 'Core inflation excludes', 'headline inflation means', statement sets pairing food/fuel exclusions with monetary relevance.
patterns.logic:
1. **Core = headline − food and fuel** — it shows the underlying trend the MPC watches alongside headline CPI.
2. Headline = the full published index; food's big CPI weight makes headline jump with supply shocks.
3. Terms: disinflation = slower inflation; deflation = negative; reflation = policy-driven recovery of prices.

example.q: **Core inflation** is best described as —
example.solution: Headline inflation **excluding food and fuel** — the steadier 'underlying' gauge that central banks read to judge persistent pressure.

patterns.name: CPI variants, IIP and core industries
patterns.howToSpot: 'DA is linked to which CPI', 'IIP measures', 'the eight core industries include', matching small facts around price and output indices.
patterns.logic:
1. CPI-IW (industrial workers, **Labour Bureau**) drives dearness allowance; CPI-AL/RL track farm and rural labourers.
2. **IIP measures output**, not prices — short-term industrial production trends.
3. Eight core industries: coal, crude oil, natural gas, refinery products, fertilisers, steel, cement, electricity — they carry a large IIP weight.

example.q: The index used for revising **dearness allowance** of central employees is —
example.solution: **CPI-IW** (Consumer Price Index for Industrial Workers), compiled by the **Labour Bureau**.

subtopics.title: Budget and fiscal policy
subtopics.concept:
### Constitutional basis
- **Article 112** — Annual Financial Statement (the Budget); **Art. 266** Consolidated Fund; **Art. 267** Contingency Fund; **Art. 265** — no tax without authority of law.
- Railway Budget merged with the Union Budget in **2017**; presented on **1 February** since 2017. **Budget 2026-27** was presented by **Nirmala Sitharaman on 1 February 2026**.

### Budget 2026-27 at a glance (BE)
| Item | Figure |
|---|---|
| Total expenditure | ₹53.47 lakh crore (₹53,47,315 cr) |
| Total receipts (ex-borrowings) | ₹36.52 lakh crore; net tax receipts ₹28.7 lakh cr |
| Borrowings (fiscal deficit in ₹) | ₹16.96 lakh crore |
| **Fiscal deficit** | **4.3% of GDP** (RE 2025-26: 4.4%) |
| Revenue deficit | 1.5% of GDP |
| Primary deficit | 0.7% of GDP |
| Capital expenditure | **₹12.2 lakh crore** (from ₹11.2 lakh cr) |
| Central debt | 55.6% of GDP; glide path to ~50% by March 2031 |
| Disinvestment target | ₹80,000 crore |
| Nominal GDP growth assumed | 10% |

New in 2026-27: **Biopharma SHAKTI** (₹10,000 cr, 5 yrs), SME Growth Fund (₹10,000 cr), Infrastructure Risk Guarantee Fund, Semiconductor Mission 2.0, Electronics Component Manufacturing outlay raised to ₹40,000 cr, ₹20,000 cr carbon-capture allocation, City Economic Regions (₹5,000 cr each), MAT cut 15% → 14%.

### Deficit definitions
| Deficit | Formula |
|---|---|
| Fiscal | Total expenditure − total receipts **excluding borrowings** |
| Revenue | Revenue expenditure − revenue receipts |
| Primary | **Fiscal deficit − interest payments** |
| Effective capital expenditure | Capex + grants for creation of capital assets |

**FRBM Act, 2003** — fiscal discipline targets; amended periodically (current glide: fiscal deficit below 4.5% of GDP, then toward ~4%).

tricks.title: Budget 2026-27 number sheet
tricks.body: Spend 53.5 • Receipts 36.5 • Borrow 16.9 (₹ lakh crore); FD 4.3% • RD 1.5% • PD 0.7%; Capex 12.2; Debt 55.6%.

example.q: Budget 2026-27 fiscal deficit?
example.solution: 4.3% of GDP (₹16.96 lakh crore).

example.q: Which article is the Annual Financial Statement?
example.solution: Article 112.

mistakes: Quoting 4.4% for FY27 — 4.4% is the 2025-26 RE; the BE 2026-27 is 4.3%.
Confusing primary deficit (fiscal − interest) with revenue deficit (revenue expenditure − receipts).
Thinking the railway budget still exists separately — merged in 2017.
subtopics.notes:
### The Budget — what the Constitution calls it
The word 'Budget' appears nowhere in the Constitution. Article 112 names it the **Annual Financial Statement** — estimated receipts and expenditure of the government for a year, laid before both Houses. Since **2017** it is presented on **1 February** (earlier: the last day of February), and the separate **Railway Budget was merged** into the general Budget the same year. A day before, the government tables the **Economic Survey** (prepared by the Department of Economic Affairs under the Chief Economic Adviser). The expenditure side appears as **Demands for Grants** per ministry; approval flows through the **Appropriation Bill** (spending) and the **Finance Bill** (tax proposals).

### The three funds
- **Consolidated Fund of India — Article 266(1)**: all revenues, loans and receipts; Parliament must authorise every withdrawal.
- **Public Account — Article 266(2)**: money held in trust — provident funds, small savings; no vote needed.
- **Contingency Fund — Article 267**: at the disposal of the **President** for unforeseen spending; corpus raised to **₹30,000 crore** in 2021.

Receipts split into **revenue** (tax, interest, dividends — non-creating) and **capital** (borrowings, disinvestment, loan recoveries); expenditure likewise splits into **revenue** (salaries, subsidies, interest) and **capital** (assets — roads, buildings, defence equipment).

### The deficits — four formulas that settle most questions
- **Revenue Deficit** = Revenue expenditure − Revenue receipts: the government borrows to run day-to-day affairs.
- **Effective Revenue Deficit** = Revenue deficit − grants for creation of capital assets: introduced in 2011-12.
- **Fiscal Deficit** = Total expenditure − Total receipts **other than borrowings**: the year's total borrowing need.
- **Primary Deficit** = Fiscal deficit − interest payments: this year's borrowing appetite, freed of past debts' interest.

The **FRBM Act, 2003** set legal limits on these deficits (amended in 2018 to add debt-GDP targets); Budgets announce a multi-year fiscal **glide path**. In matching questions, fiscal deficit always 'includes' the others' interest burden — the largest single expenditure head is interest payment, followed by subsidies and defence.

### Quick revision
- Budget = Annual Financial Statement (Art 112); presented 1 February since 2017; Railway Budget merged 2017.
- Funds: Consolidated 266(1), Public Account 266(2), Contingency 267 (President; ₹30,000 crore corpus).
- Economic Survey: day before, Dept of Economic Affairs; Appropriation Bill = spending, Finance Bill = taxes.
- RD = Rev Exp − Rev Rec; ERD = RD − capital-asset grants; FD = Total Exp − (Rec − borrowings); PD = FD − interest.
- FRBM Act 2003; interest payments are the largest expenditure head.

patterns.name: Deficit arithmetic
patterns.howToSpot: Expenditure, receipts and interest figures are given and one deficit is asked; or a relationship ('primary deficit is negative because') is tested.
patterns.logic:
1. Fiscal deficit = total expenditure − total receipts **excluding borrowings**.
2. Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − **interest payments** (it can be negative — a primary surplus).
3. Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts; plug the numbers in one step and check units (lakh crore).

example.q: Total expenditure is ₹45 lakh crore and receipts excluding borrowings ₹39 lakh crore. The **fiscal deficit** is —
example.solution: 45 − 39 = **₹6 lakh crore** — exactly the amount the government must borrow this year.

patterns.name: Budget structure, articles and funds
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which article is the Annual Financial Statement', 'the Contingency Fund is at whose disposal', matching each fund with its article and purpose.
patterns.logic:
1. Article 112 = Annual Financial Statement (the constitutional 'Budget'); Article 266(1) = Consolidated Fund; 266(2) = Public Account; Article 267 = Contingency Fund.
2. Contingency Fund = **President's disposal**; Consolidated Fund = no withdrawal without **Parliament's vote**; Public Account = no vote needed.
3. 'Budget' is not a constitutional word — options saying 'Budget is defined in Article 112' are wrong.

example.q: The **Contingency Fund of India** is placed at the disposal of —
example.solution: The **President** (Article 267) — used for unforeseen expenditure, later regularised by Parliament; corpus ₹30,000 crore.

patterns.name: Revenue vs capital, effective revenue deficit
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which is a capital receipt', 'effective revenue deficit excludes', statements classifying disinvestment, borrowings, grants.
patterns.logic:
1. Capital receipts: **borrowings, disinvestment proceeds, recovery of loans** — they either create liability or cut assets.
2. Capital expenditure: roads, buildings, defence equipment, loans to states. Revenue expenditure: salaries, subsidies, interest.
3. **Effective revenue deficit = revenue deficit − grants for creation of capital assets** (introduced 2011-12).

example.q: Which of the following is a **capital receipt**?
example.solution: **Disinvestment proceeds** — selling government equity reduces assets; borrowings and loan recoveries are the other classic capital receipts.

patterns.name: FRBM and the fiscal glide path
patterns.howToSpot: 'The FRBM Act was passed in', statements on deficit targets, debt-GDP anchors, the meaning of a glide path in Budget speeches.
patterns.logic:
1. **FRBM Act 2003** — fiscal responsibility and budget management: legal deficit targets, amended in 2018 (debt anchors added).
2. Budgets declare a **fiscal glide path** — a year-by-year path for fiscal deficit as a share of GDP.
3. Interest payments, not subsidies, are the single largest revenue-expenditure head — a favourite 'true statement' fact.

example.q: The **FRBM Act**, which sets legal targets for deficits and debt, was enacted in —
example.solution: **2003** — the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act disciplines deficits; a 2018 amendment added debt-to-GDP anchors.

patterns.name: Budget process, dates and documents
patterns.howToSpot: 'Since which year is the Budget presented on 1 February', 'the Economic Survey is tabled when', 'the Railway Budget was merged in', questions on Demands for Grants / appropriation.
patterns.logic:
1. From **2017**: presentation on **1 February** and the **Railway Budget merged** into the general Budget.
2. **Economic Survey** comes the day before (Dept of Economic Affairs / Chief Economic Adviser).
3. Spending needs **Demands for Grants** per ministry, then an **Appropriation Bill**; taxes move via the **Finance Bill**.

example.q: The **Economic Survey** is presented —
example.solution: A day **before the Union Budget**, by the Department of Economic Affairs; it reviews the economy's performance and outlook.

subtopics.title: Taxation and GST
subtopics.concept:
### Direct vs indirect taxes
| Direct | Indirect |
|---|---|
| Income tax, corporate tax, capital gains, STT; burden cannot be shifted | GST, customs duty; burden shifted to consumer |

Direct-tax code change: the **Income-tax Act, 2025** replaces the 1961 Act **from 1 April 2026** — 536 sections in 23 chapters and a single **"tax year"** replacing assessment/previous year. Under the new regime (FY 2025-26 Budget), income up to ₹12 lakh attracts no tax (₹12.75 lakh for salaried with standard deduction).

### GST
- Introduced **1 July 2017** by the **101st Constitutional Amendment** — Articles **246A** (power to tax), **269A** (inter-state apportionment), **279A** (**GST Council**).
- **GST Council**: chaired by the **Union Finance Minister**; Union MoS Finance + State finance ministers; quorum = half; decisions by **3/4th weighted majority (Centre 1/3, States 2/3)**.
- **GST 2.0** (56th Council, 3 Sep 2025; effective **22 Sep 2025**): slabs collapsed to **5% and 18%**, plus a **40% demerit rate** for sin/luxury goods (12% and 28% abolished; compensation cess ended except pan masala & tobacco products). Small cars, ACs, TVs moved to 18%.
- GST compensation to States ran Jul 2017 – Jun 2022 under the Act.

### Other revenue markers
LTCG on equities 12.5% (> ₹1.25 lakh) since Budget 2024; STT raised in Budget 2026; buybacks taxed as capital gains for holders with promoter-level buyback tax. Customs is the only major indirect tax outside GST.

example.q: Which article created the GST Council?
example.solution: Article 279A (101st Amendment, 2016).

tricks.title: GST 2.0 slab story
tricks.body: Two working slabs — 5 (merit) and 18 (standard) — with 40 kept aside for sin/luxury; 12% and 28% abolished on 22 Sep 2025.

example.q: GST on a small car now?
example.solution: 18% (moved from 28% plus cess).

tricks.title: Tax-year switch
tricks.body: Income-tax Act, 2025 → effective 1 April 2026; one 'tax year' replaces previous/assessment year pair; 536 sections, 23 chapters.

example.q: From which income year does 'Tax Year' apply?
example.solution: FY 2026-27, called Tax Year 2026-27.

mistakes: Calling STT an indirect tax — it is a direct tax on transactions.
Assuming compensation cess continues on all goods — it ended 22 Sep 2025 except pan masala/tobacco lines.
Mixing the GST Council's 3/4 weighted majority with a 'simple majority of members'.
subtopics.notes:
### Direct vs indirect — the master divide
**Direct taxes** fall on the person who pays them: **income tax, corporate tax, securities transaction tax (STT), capital-gains tax** — progressivity built in, burden not shiftable. **Indirect taxes** are paid to the government but shifted to consumers through prices: **GST, customs duty, excise duty on petroleum and alcohol, stamp duties** — they are regressive (the rich and poor pay the same rate on a good) but easy to collect. Corporation tax and income tax are the top two direct-tax heads; GST the biggest indirect one. **Agricultural income** stays outside income tax (taxing it is a state power).

### GST — one nation, one tax
The **101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016** created GST, effective from **1 July 2017**; it is a **destination-based consumption tax** subsuming excise, service tax, VAT, CST, entry tax and luxury tax. Constitutional pegs: **Article 246A** (power to legislate), **269A** (inter-state/IGST apportionment), **279A** (**GST Council**). The Council — Union **Finance Minister as chair**, with the Union Minister of State for Finance and state finance ministers — decides rates and rules by a **three-fourths weighted majority**: Centre holds **one-third** of votes, states together **two-thirds**. Structure: **CGST** (Centre) + **SGST** (state) on intra-state sales; **IGST** on inter-state and imports; the **GSTN** runs the IT backbone.

**Slabs after the GST 2.0 reform (Council decision of 3 September 2025, effective 22 September 2025)**: two principal slabs — **5% (merit)** and **18% (standard)** — plus a **40% rate for demerit goods** (tobacco, pan masala, some luxury items); the old 12% slab was abolished and the 28% rate phased out into the 40% demerit track. Exemptions survive (unprocessed food, education, health). Compensation cess continues on specified demerit goods, now aligned to the 40% rate.

### Income tax — the new code
The **Income-tax Act, 2025** — passed in August 2025, **effective 1 April 2026** — replaces the Income-tax Act of 1961. Its signature reform is the single '**tax year**' replacing the twin concepts of previous year and assessment year; the Act has 536 sections in 23 chapters, in plainer language. Filing stays annual; a default **new regime** with lower slab rates but few deductions coexists with the older optional regime. **Tax devolution** to states flows through the **Finance Commission** (Article 280), the constitutional arbiter of the vertical split.

### Quick revision
- Direct: income, corporate, STT, capital gains. Indirect: GST, customs, excise (petroleum/alcohol), stamp.
- GST: 101st Amendment, 1 July 2017; Articles 246A / 269A / 279A; Council chaired by Union FM, 3/4 majority, Centre 1/3 : states 2/3.
- CGST + SGST intra-state; IGST inter-state; GSTN = IT network.
- GST 2.0: 22 September 2025 — slabs 5% and 18%, 40% demerit, 12% abolished.
- Income-tax Act 2025: effective 1 April 2026, 'tax year' replaces previous/assessment year.
- Agricultural income — no income tax; devolution via Finance Commission.

patterns.name: GST Council and constitutional articles
patterns.howToSpot: 'Article 279A deals with', 'who chairs the GST Council', 'the Centre has what share of votes', matching GST articles and Council facts.
patterns.logic:
1. Articles in a line: **246A** = power to tax, **269A** = IGST on inter-state trade, **279A** = GST Council.
2. Council: Union **Finance Minister chairs**; members include the Union MoS (Finance) and state finance ministers.
3. Decisions: **3/4 weighted majority — Centre 1/3, all states together 2/3**.

example.q: Under the GST framework, the **GST Council** is constituted under —
example.solution: **Article 279A**, inserted by the 101st Amendment — chaired by the Union Finance Minister, with decisions by a three-fourths weighted majority (Centre one-third, states two-thirds).

patterns.name: GST launch, structure and the 2025 slab reform
patterns.howToSpot: 'GST was introduced from', 'which article inserted GST', 'the new GST slabs are', questions naming CGST/SGST/IGST and the 22 September 2025 change.
patterns.logic:
1. Launch: **1 July 2017**, via the **101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016**; destination-based.
2. Structure: CGST + SGST intra-state; **IGST** inter-state and on imports; GSTN = IT backbone.
3. From **22 September 2025** (Council decision 3 September 2025): slabs **5% and 18%**, a **40% demerit rate**, **12% abolished** — the GST 2.0 reform.

example.q: After the GST 2.0 reform effective 22 September 2025, the principal GST slabs are —
example.solution: **5% (merit) and 18% (standard)**, with a **40% rate for demerit goods**; the 12% slab was abolished and the 28% rate retired into the demerit track.

patterns.name: Direct vs indirect classification
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which is a direct tax', 'which tax cannot be shifted', options mixing customs, corporate tax, GST, STT.
patterns.logic:
1. Direct = burden on the payer: **income tax, corporate tax, STT, capital gains**.
2. Indirect = shifted to consumers: **GST, customs, excise (petroleum, alcohol), stamp duties**.
3. Remember the constitutional split: GST article 246A; agricultural income outside income tax.

example.q: Which of the following is a **direct tax**?
example.solution: **Corporate tax** — levied directly on company profits with no shifting; GST, customs and stamp duty are indirect.

patterns.name: Income-tax Act 2025 and the tax year
patterns.howToSpot: 'The new Income-tax Act is effective from', 'the concept of tax year replaces', questions on the 2025 code replacing the 1961 Act.
patterns.logic:
1. **Income-tax Act, 2025** — passed August 2025, **effective 1 April 2026**, replacing the 1961 Act.
2. Single '**tax year**' replaces previous year + assessment year; 536 sections, 23 chapters, simpler drafting.
3. Devolution of taxes to states = **Finance Commission (Article 280)**.

example.q: The **Income-tax Act, 2025** became operative from —
example.solution: **1 April 2026** — replacing the 1961 Act and introducing the single '**tax year**' in place of the previous-year/assessment-year pair.

patterns.name: Tax bases, exemption and devolution facts
patterns.howToSpot: 'Agricultural income is taxed by', 'corporation tax contributes most to', which head dominates direct-tax collections, devolution mechanics.
patterns.logic:
1. **Agricultural income** — outside income tax; taxing it belongs to states.
2. Direct-tax collections are led by **corporation tax and personal income tax**; GST leads the indirect side.
3. Centre-state sharing runs through the **Finance Commission's** award; cesses and surcharges sit outside the divisible pool — a standard statement question.

example.q: Regarding **agricultural income**, the income-tax law —
example.solution: Leaves it untaxed: taxing agricultural income is a **state** power, so it stays outside the Income-tax Act's net.

subtopics.notes:
### Reading a scheme question
Every scheme question tests four hooks: **launch year, ministry, benefit/eligibility, and purpose**. Learn them as one line each; the exam never asks beyond these. Monthly 'new scheme' news changes, but the flagships below are permanent fixtures of SSC/Railway/Banking papers.

### Livelihood and employment
- **MGNREGA** (Act 2005, operational 2006): 100 days of guaranteed wage employment per rural household — replaced by **VB-G RAM G** from **1 July 2026**, raising the guarantee to **125 days a year** with weekly wage payments.
- **DAY-NRLM** (2011): rural livelihoods through women's self-help groups; urban twin DAY-NULM (2014).
- **PM SVANidhi** (2020): working-capital loans for street vendors.
- **Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana** umbrella covers both livelihood missions (Ministry of Rural Development / MoHUA).

### Financial inclusion and credit
- **PM Jan Dhan Yojana** — launched **28 August 2014**: zero-balance bank accounts, RuPay card, overdraft facility; the world's largest financial-inclusion drive.
- **MUDRA Yojana** (**8 April 2015**): collateral-free micro-loans in three tiers — **Shishu (up to ₹50,000), Kishor (₹50,000-5 lakh), Tarun (₹5-10 lakh)**.
- **Atal Pension Yojana** (2015): guaranteed pension for unorganised workers aged 18-40.
- **PMSBY** (accident insurance, ₹20/year, cover ₹2 lakh) and **PMJJBY** (life insurance) — the two Jan Suraksha schemes.

### Agriculture and rural
- **PM-KISAN** (Feb 2019): **₹6,000 a year** to landholding farmer families, paid in three DBT instalments.
- **PM Fasal Bima Yojana** (2016): subsidised crop insurance; **e-NAM** (2016): unified electronic mandi.
- **Kisan Credit Card** (1998): short-term crop credit; **PM-KUSUM**: solar pumps for farmers.

### Health, water, housing, fuel
- **Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY** (**23 September 2018**): health cover of **₹5 lakh per family a year** for secondary and tertiary hospitalisation; **ABHA** is its digital health-ID arm, with the **Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission** (September 2021) building the health stack.
- **Jal Jeevan Mission** (**August 2019**, 'Har Ghar Jal'): functional household tap connections.
- **Swachh Bharat Mission** (**2 October 2014**): sanitation and ODF drive; **POSHAN Abhiyaan** (2018): nutrition mission under the WCD ministry.
- **PM Awas Yojana** (urban 2015; Gramin 2016): pucca houses; **PM Ujjwala Yojana** (1 May 2016): free LPG connections to women of poor households.

### Industry and skills
- **Make in India** (25 September 2014); **Startup India** (16 January 2016, DPIIT recognition and tax holidays); **Skill India / PMKVY** (2015); **Production-Linked Incentive (PLI)** schemes (2020); **PM Gati Shakti** (October 2021) national infrastructure master plan; **UDAN** (2016) regional air connectivity.

### Quick revision
- VB-G RAM G (1 July 2026): 125 days, weekly wages — replaced MGNREGA.
- Jan Dhan 28-8-2014; MUDRA 8-4-2015 (Shishu/Kishor/Tarun); APY 2015; PMSBY/PMJJBY insurance.
- PM-KISAN ₹6,000/yr in 3 instalments (2019); Fasal Bima 2016; KCC 1998.
- Ayushman PM-JAY ₹5 lakh/family (2018); JJM 2019; SBM 2-10-2014; Ujjwala 1-5-2016; PMAY 2015/16.
- Make in India 25-9-2014; Startup India 16-1-2016; Gati Shakti 2021; PLI 2020.

patterns.name: Scheme ↔ ministry ↔ launch year
patterns.howToSpot: 'X scheme was launched in which year', 'which ministry runs X', matching schemes with 2014-2021 launch dates.
patterns.logic:
1. Pin the dates: SBM 2-10-2014; Jan Dhan 28-8-2014; MUDRA 8-4-2015; Startup 16-1-2016; JJM 2019; PM-KISAN 2019; Gati Shakti 2021.
2. Ministry pairs: PMAY-U/Day-NULM/SVANidhi — MoHUA; NRLM/NREGA-line — Rural Development; POSHAN — WCD; UDAN — Civil Aviation.
3. Anchor on the year first; the ministry usually follows from the scheme's subject.

example.q: **Startup India** was launched in —
example.solution: **January 2016** (16 January) — DPIIT recognition, tax holidays and a fund-of-funds for startups.

patterns.name: Scheme ↔ benefit ↔ eligibility
patterns.howToSpot: '₹6,000 a year is paid under', '₹5 lakh health cover belongs to', matching the benefit figure with the right scheme.
patterns.logic:
1. Money anchors: PM-KISAN **₹6,000/yr (3 instalments)**; PM-JAY **₹5 lakh/family/yr**; MUDRA tiers ₹50k / ₹5 lakh / ₹10 lakh; APY 18-40 age window.
2. PMSBY = accident cover ₹20/yr; PMJJBY = life cover; both ₹2 lakh protection.
3. Match the rupee figure or the age/eligibility first — it eliminates three options at once.

example.q: A guaranteed **₹6,000 per year to landholding farmer families** is paid under —
example.solution: **PM-KISAN** (2019) — direct benefit transfer in three instalments.

patterns.name: Employment and livelihood schemes
patterns.howToSpot: 'How many days of employment does X guarantee', 'which scheme replaced MGNREGA', statements on NRLM self-help groups or SVANidhi vendors.
patterns.logic:
1. The wage-employment line: MGNREGA (2005 Act, 100 days) → **VB-G RAM G from 1 July 2026, 125 days, weekly wages**.
2. Livelihood line: DAY-NRLM (2011) builds **women SHGs** in villages; DAY-NULM (2014) covers urban livelihoods.
3. PM SVANidhi (2020) = **street vendors'** collateral-free working capital.

example.q: The rural employment guarantee that replaced **MGNREGA** from 1 July 2026 is —
example.solution: **VB-G RAM G** — it lifted the guaranteed days per rural household per year to **125** and moved wages to weekly payment.

patterns.name: Financial inclusion schemes
patterns.howToSpot: 'Zero-balance accounts under', 'Shishu-Kishor-Tarun belong to', which scheme insures against accidents for ₹20 a year.
patterns.logic:
1. **Jan Dhan (28-8-2014)** = accounts + RuPay + overdraft; the flagship of financial inclusion.
2. **MUDRA (8-4-2015)** tiers: Shishu ≤ ₹50,000; Kishor ₹50,000-5 lakh; Tarun ₹5-10 lakh — collateral-free micro-credit.
3. **APY** = pension for 18-40 unorganised workers; **PMSBY** = ₹2 lakh accident cover at ₹20/year.

example.q: The MUDRA loan categories **Shishu, Kishor and Tarun** refer to —
example.solution: Collateral-free micro-loan sizes: **up to ₹50,000, ₹50,000-5 lakh and ₹5-10 lakh** respectively.

patterns.name: Health, water, housing and fuel schemes
patterns.howToSpot: 'Har Ghar Jal belongs to', 'the LPG connection scheme is', '₹5 lakh hospitalisation cover', matching social-sector schemes with purposes.
patterns.logic:
1. Health: **PM-JAY ₹5 lakh/family** (2018); digital arm **ABDM (2021)** with ABHA IDs.
2. Water and sanitation: **JJM 2019** (tap connections); **SBM 2-10-2014** (toilets/ODF).
3. Housing and fuel: **PMAY** (2015 urban / 2016 rural); **Ujjwala 1-5-2016** (free LPG to women).

example.q: '**Har Ghar Jal**' — functional tap water connections to every rural household — is the goal of —
example.solution: **Jal Jeevan Mission**, launched in **August 2019** under the Jal Shakti ministry.
